newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour's Brown takes tough inflation stand.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour's Brown takes tough inflation stand.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer-in-waiting Gordon Brown said on Friday that a Labour government would be tough on inflation and set interest rates to hit the party's 2.5 percent target.
"People are right to say we must avoid the inflationary pressures that could exist at this time in the economic cycle," he told Reuters Financial Television.

He was speaking as exit polls and early results in the election suggested Labour was on its way to a landslide victory over the ruling Conservatives, with Brown likely to be the next finance minister.
Markets are focused on a monetary meeting between the finance minister and Bank of England Governor Eddie George scheduled for May 7, which could well result in a small rise in interest rates.
Brown said if Labour leader Tony Blair confirmed him as chancellor, he would discuss whether the meeting would take place.
The British economy is growing strongly, with consumer spending particularly robust.
Economic data have shown wage pressures building in the services sector, and many economists have said an interest rate rise is needed quickly to keep a lid on earnings growth.
Brown refused to comment on the appropriate level of rates but repeated the party's commitment to the inflation target.
"I will stick by the inflation target that we have set down. We have always said we will set monetary policy in that respect."
He said tough fiscal rules and spending ceilings laid out during the election campaign were sacrosanct.
Brown has pledged to match tight Conservative spending targets for the next two years and leave income tax rates untouched.

Earlier, Brown told reporters a budget will be held within two months to implement a planned windfall tax on privatised utilities, the proceeds of which Labour says will help 250,000 young people into work.
The budget will also cut VAT sales tax on fuel to five percent from eight, he said.
"We will endeavour to tackle the problems of unemployment and also to achieve a lasting recovery," he said.
Brown refused to be drawn on on the issue of a single European currency. He said the option of UK membership was being kept open and a referendum would be held before joining.

To cheers from Labour Party loyalists, Brown left the vote centre to fly back to London. But a party aide said Brown would not join the celebration parties underway in the capital, but would start work immediately.
